Deep Learning-based Time Series Models, such as Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs), have been highly effective in various forecasting tasks. TCNs utilize a convolutional approach that allows them to efficiently process temporal data and accommodate varying time series durations. However, employing TCNs in real-world applications is often hindered due to the absence of open-source trimmers. Trimbers are critical tools that enable the efficient reduction of hyperparameter complexity in high-capacity models such as TCNs, enabling them to be more readily deployed in limited-resource environments. In this paper, we introduce a lightweight, open-source TCN trimmer called Trimming In Time (PIT). Unlike explicit model trimmers which can complicate training by intermingling trimming and training processes, PIT is a separate processing step that maintains consistent performance with dedicated model trimmers. We demonstrate PIT's efficacy by conducting thorough experiments under constrained computational budgets, and the project is now available on GitHub under the permissive MIT License. Furthermore, we introduce the Forecasting CodeSearch to facilitate the evaluation of coding solutions aimed at accelerating and enhancing the performance of time series forecasting codes. This code search database can be accessed via CodeSearch. Additionally, we introduce an alternative, lightweight version of TCN called Thin TCN (T-TCN), which serves as a code search target. T-TCN, obtained via lightweight model construction using the PIT trimer, achieves comparable performance to regular TCNs at a fraction of the parameter count. T-TCN has been incorporated into the CodeSearch database as a code search target for those seeking to evaluate the performance of thin, high-performance time series forecasting models. We anticipate this code will be useful for monitoring the development of compact neural network models across various datasets in the forecasting domain. We invite researchers to submit their own code for inclusion in the CodeSearch database. We employed the CodeSearch database to evaluate the performance of thin, high-performance time series forecasting models and the results of our experiments have been published in the paper titled "Evaluating Model Compression in Time Series Forecasting" which can be accessed via the CodeSearch website. This involves first establishing that the symmetry group of the 21 remaining symmetries acts freely on a specific configuration of the 27 lines. With this action in place, the number of bitangents can be determined using a combinatorial formula and the properties of the Abelian variety associated with the 27 lines. Ultimately, this approach enables us to relate the number of bitangents to a specific divisor on this variety. As a further development, we explore how to count bitangents on a general quartic surface over the real numbers, introducing a real signed tally that reflects the configuration of bitangents consisting of pairs of lines with opposite orientations. This extension of the previous calculation demonstrates that there are $16\cdot 27$ such bitangents. All the calculations presented are preconditions for a more complex scenario involving a duality-based approach and a higher-dimensional analog of the 27 lines theorem. This leads to a calculation of the number of a type of hypersurface that can be parameterized using a cubic form over a quadratic base. This parameterization enables us to determine that the total number of such hypersurfaces is $2^{27}$. Building upon this result, we are able to prove that there are $16\cdot 27$ real signed bitangents on a general quartic surface over the real numbers. This proof relies on a deeper understanding of the properties of the Abelian variety associated with the 27 lines and its relationship to the real signed tally of bitangents. Finally, we note that in the process of developing this proof, we are to prove a more general statement that encompasses this specific instance. However, the general statement relies on a assumption that the associated Abelian variety has a specific property. While this property holds true for the Abelian variety associated with the 27 lines, it does not hold true in a more general scenario. Consequently, the general scenario requires a different approach, one that involves a more complex calculation that utilizes a different method to determine the number of bitangents. Ultimately, this approach confirms that the number of bitangents on a general quartic surface is $126$. This result is consistent with a previous study that reached the same conclusion

While such datasets are valuable tools for system development, they have limitations. For instance, they might not account for subtle inaccuracies common in human-generated descriptions. Furthermore, they may not consider whether the descriptions provided are sufficient to capture the entire scene or just a particular aspect. Additionally, such datasets usually focus on evaluating the accuracy of individual descriptions rather than the overall description of an image. To address these concerns, this work introduces an innovative method to gather more comprehensive human feedback. Instead of relying on mere rating scales, humans provide detailed information on whether each word in the description is precise or covers an entire scene or specific image region. This richer data allows for a more nuanced analysis of the accuracy, completeness, and coherence of automatic descriptions. The advantages of this approach are demonstrated using a widely used dataset, with results showing significant improvements in evaluation metrics as well as increased sensitivity to description inaccuracies. Neural machine translation systems rely on massive parallel corpora and the paradigms of parallel and sequential translation have distinct requirements for data. Current neural machine translation models are typically trained on parallel data alone. We propose a novel interpretation of neural machine translation using a monolingual translation archive that enables models to generate targeted language understood as a derived meaning from the source text. We suggest a type of corpus known as targeted parallel corpora, which are parallel corpora that convey a specific meaning, and demonstrate how these can be created from sequential parallel corpora. Furthermore, we introduce the Token-level Controlled Generation (TCG) framework, which can create targeted parallel corpora and produce high-quality outputs when evaluated on the LAMBODA dataset. The TCG framework involves modifying a monolingual translation archive with targeted labels through token-level filtering and subsequent multi-round backward generation from the derived meaning to the source and target languages. The modified archive is then utilized to train models to produce targeted language. The models that emerge from this process excel in few-shot learning tasks according to our experiments. The models we trained for the TCG task also apply to other tasks such as text classification and the generation of targeted text classification labels. The techniques we explored to enhance the quality of generation, namely the application of pre-trained text classifiers on the source language and the introduction of noise into the targeted labels, are equally effective. Human beings can quickly grasp new concepts based on limited examples, which has long been observed to result from a combination of inherent assumptions and the learning process.  Despite significant advancements in deep learning, recognizing new classes from minimal labeled data remains a challenge.  A prominent issue here is that deep models, by nature, combine features from all classes in the training dataset to output classification results, which inevitably hinders their performance in later class predictions.  A recent approach known as differentiable dense prototype learning attempts to address this by introducing prototypes that are trained in an efficient, end-to-end manner. Nevertheless, this method still falls short because it selects the same basis functions for all classes and ignores the unique characteristics of individual classes.  Instead of equating the descriptors with the means of all classes as done previously, our framework proposes a new scoring function that can extract unique prototypes for each new class from minimal labeled data.  The score of a sample for a class is calculated as the dot product of the prototype and the basis functions associated with that sample.  To accommodate this change, our method chooses a different set of basis functions for each new class and learns the prototypes in a two-stage process.  Experimental results show our approach outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods on few-shot classification, demonstrating that the performance boost results from the ability to extract unique prototypes from minimal labeled data.  The proposed approach also yields superior performance when compared to the baseline using standard deep models on several challenges including few-shot segmentation, pose estimation and classification. The foundation theorem is a significant and extensively utilized result in the theory of finite Coxeter groups, particularly within the realm of geometric combinatorics. It possesses numerous significant consequences, including the combinatorial classification of Coxeter groups, the exotic nature of finite Coxeter groups, and a landmark result on the universal accessibility of finite Coxeter groups. This paper extends the foundation theorem to a previously unstudied class of Coxeter groups defined by the B-type, which includes infinite hyperbolic groups, among others. Some implications of this extension are also established, along with a powerful accessibility result for a broad family of these groups. Moreover, this paper introduces a novel, explicit representation of the foundation theorem for the classical B-type Coxeter groups. Finally, it proves a combinatorial classification theorem for the finite B-type Coxeter groups. To better reflect real-life conversations, we propose a more complex framework that incorporates many possible conversation paths. This new framework, which we call MultiTalk, starts with a central hub from which the conversation can diverge in several directions. Each branch represents a unique topic or area of discussion. Unlike previous testing methods, MultiTalk features a high degree of branching, with multiple opportunities for conversational agents to respond. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this new framework, we also developed a data set comprised of over 150 starting messages, along with their corresponding appropriate responses. This data set, which we call MultiTalk-Dataset, can be utilized to assess the proficiency of state-of-the-art conversational models in engaging with others through a variety of topics and subjects. Leveraging this dataset and testing it with state-of-the-art models like T5 and Unity, we showed that simple fine-tuning methods can yield very good results, producing highly acceptable responses according to human evaluators. These models performed notably better than models that had not been adapted to this testing method. Furthermore, when applied to real-world chat applications, these models exhibited superior performance when compared to their unoptimized counterparts. We introduce a novel computational approach that enables rapid, highly accurate n-body simulations tailored to various gravitational theories, with a specific focus on conformal coupling models. This method is distinct from typical Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey-like simulations, as it conducts exhaustive, particle-based simulations to produce realistic galaxy distributions. Our technique modifies the standard gravitational field equation by incorporating a Weyl tensor-based approximation, which leverages a computationally efficient framework developed by Bardeen et al. We examine the theoretical framework and computational strategy of our model, and present a set of conformal coupling-based simulations that explore the effects of these alternative gravities on galaxy formation and structure. Conversely, our results indicate that generic altered gravity scenarios can be effectively discerned through our rapid n-body simulations, specifically those featuring weakly coupled conformal gravity, without needing extensive, traditional n-body simulations. Ultimately, such a method holds significant potential to inform and shape the interpretation of galaxy data within the context of various gravitational theories. The implementation of this approach as a multi-physics simulation tool, combining gravitational field calculations with galaxy formation models, is also discussed. This technique is now an open source framework available at https://github.com/fgalvez/FASTS and can be used to conduct a wide range of generic altered gravity simulations at a fraction of the traditional cost. Additionally, a set of 32 new high-resolution image files in PNG format, derived from our standard, fast and standard simulations, have been uploaded to the Los Alamos Archive under the banner https://lanl.gov/index.php/list/view/227325. Furthermore, a set of 16 corresponding VOFIT files are available at https://github.com/fgalvez/VOFIT-FAST. These data products provide a visual representation of galaxy density, mass and spin fields resulting from our fast and standard simulations, and can be fit using an adapted version of the VOFIT software available at https://github.com/fgalvez/VOFIT-FAST. This issue of whether fast, high-accuracy simulations can capture the complexity of galaxy formation and structure is further explored, with a specific examination of how matter distribution is influenced by varying cosmological parameters, such as the power spectrum amplitude, primordial perturbation type and initial seed configuration. Furthermore, a comparative analysis is conducted between our fast, conventional and lagrangian simulations, with a focus on identifying any discrepancies in the resulting galaxy populations, as well as a validation of our fast simulations against traditional n-body simulations, using a range of analytical and numerical metrics.

We present a novel method for detecting multiple types of dynamic states, including travelling chimeras and synchronized groups, in complex networks of interconnected neurons. Our approach is highly resilient to data inaccuracies and obfuscations, offering a clear and concise description of the underlying dynamics. Unlike existing methods that rely heavily on detailed numerical simulations and specialized software, our approach is simple and easily executed using widely available mathematical tools and software. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method through analysis of a range of artificial network datasets and a real brain dataset, showcasing its ability to accurately identify travelling chimeras, synchronized groups, and other complex dynamics from limited and realistically obtainable short data samples. This method significantly lowers the barrier for entry into the advanced field of complex network dynamics analysis, making it possible for researchers to successfully identify and describe the intricate dynamics of large-scale neural networks from compact, achievable data samples. Furthermore, our method fetches a relatively modest computational price, making it an extremely useful asset for the field. This study examines the capability of a specific deep learning model, U-Net, in using adult heart MRI data to segment hearts with rare congenital heart defects. We investigated the potential of transferring this knowledge to provide pre-surgical mappings of the heart anatomy for individuals born with these defects. Our experiments demonstrated that despite significant differences in heart morphology, U-Net can accurately automate segmentation for three common defects - tetralogy of Fallot, transposition of the great arteries, and truncus arteriosus - when trained on a limited dataset of 50 cases per condition, as validated by both automated evaluation and expert cardiologists. However, the results also indicated that U-Net may not entirely mimic expert knowledge of heart anatomy, particularly in areas near surgical interventions. To address this, we explored the use of parent-child U-Nets, a form of anatomically-informed reconstruction, and observed further improvements in both evaluation metrics and medical expert assessments. The proposed method we developed demonstrates potential value in providing personalized heart segmentations for patients with rare congenital heart defects from standard adult heart MRI scans. The implementation of this approach in clinical settings may facilitate the integration of AI-driven medical expertise in cardiac surgery planning. The integration of PICO (patient, intervention, comparison, outcome) statements would serve as a useful guide for the development of such a protocol. The high degree of variability among individuals born with rare congenital heart defects underscores the necessity of conducting further research with a broader, more diverse participant pool. The study we present here makes notable contributions to the development of a robust, widely applicable medical AI technology, and we believe that our results may also be relevant to other areas where the transfer of expertise between similar but distinct populations is a critical consideration. The ultimate challenge in developing gravitational wave sensors lies in achieving a high frequency responsiveness. Current sensors employ the Sagnac interferometer design, relying on the sensing of vibration differences across opposing light paths. However, a novel'sloshing Sagnac' interferometer design is presented here, leveraging a container filled with a refractive liquid to drastically increase its response sensitivity in the high frequency range. By modeling the container as a cavity and incorporating a layer of absorbent to control liquid oscillations, the sensor's noise in the high frequency range can be reduced through control of the cavity's Q factor. As a result, the new design surpasses the current limitations of the Sagnac interferometer in terms of vibration sensing in the high frequency range. Furthermore, the integration of a gravitational wave detector's readout system is also demonstrated, enabling real-time observation of heart beats and breathing. The improved responsiveness of the sloshing Sagnac design makes it an attractive solution for multi-frequency gravitational wave detection. The novel design may also find utility in other sensitive vibration measurements, such as planet hunting in exoplanet systems or seismic monitoring of biological samples. The code and methodology employed in the research are presented in the attached code file. The research indicates that the noise in the new design is dominated by the readout system in the high frequency range. The measured vibration resolution of the new system is roughly double the current limit of the Sagnac interferometer. The research also implies that the scalability of the new design is limited due to the restriction that the light path and the container dimensions must both fit within the required coherence length. The future potential of the new design is for multi-frequency gravitational wave detection, where the MESA detector, with its improved high frequency responsiveness, could surpass the current limitations of the current generation of large scale detectors. The code attached to the paper can be found at the following link: https://github.com/anderson-lab/sloshing-sagnac. Research into large-scale multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems is a highly active area, and a promising approach is the XL-MIMO protocol, characterized by non-intersecting visibility areas. However, determining the throughput of this system is a complex challenge due to the intricate relationships between visibility areas, interference, and the number of antennas. To tackle this issue, a method was developed to model the visibility areas around each base station antenna as overlapping spheres, which enabled the derivation of an approximate formula for the throughput calculation. Utilizing this model, a higher throughput was observed with a greater antenna spacing, although this resulted in increased interference between spheres. Interestingly, the optimal spacing between antennas was found to be twice the cube root of the product of the number of antennas and the signal-to-noise ratio. Furthermore, this optimal spacing led to a significant increase in throughput, reaching as high as 300% more than the standard protocol. To validate these findings, a simulation model was established, which demonstrated a clear correlation between the number of antennas and the increase in throughput across a variety of scenarios. However, the optimal spacing was shown to yield better results than the standard protocol, especially in scenarios with a limited number of antennas. Additionally, the optimal spacing was discovered to provide a more substantial increase in throughput for certain system configurations. The paper also explores the implications of its findings and identifies areas for further research into the performance of large-scale MIMO systems. By simulating these substances at the level of individual electrons, we've discovered a more realistic atomic framework that aligns with experimental observations. As a result, we suggest that certain paraelectric perovskites can exhibit ferroelectric behavior due to an alternative structural arrangement, contradicting the long-held belief that this arrangement is exclusively found in ferroelectric perovskites. This finding is relevant to improving the performance of electronic devices used for storing digital information.

In group-III monochalcogenides, particularly in BS, we find a unique, heavily hybridized two-dimensional edge state that resembles the Dirac cone of graphene but with increased binding energy and a distinct angular dispersion. This phenomenon occurs naturally within these materials due to their inherent structure, which incorporates a honeycomb lattice constructed from adjacent binary crystals. A prominent 2D state then emerges when a strong link is introduced between these binary layers, causing the edge state to cross the Fermi level and resulting in anomalous Hall conductivity. By examining the spectral properties of the two-dimensional edge state, we identify a significant electronic transition as the chemical potential shifts from the valence to the conduction band. This transition is marked by a change in the Berry curvature and a shift in the orbital from being primarily p-like to being mostly s-like. The proposed link modifies the lattice parameters, leading to a reduction in the lattice constant and the bond length, while increasing the spin-orbit coupling. These changes cause a rotation of the quasiparticle's orbital and a shift in the edge state's center of mass, influencing its energetic location. Consequently, the electronic transition becomes an adjustable property that can be fine-tuned by varying the link strength, the spin-orbit coupling, and the quasiparticle's mass. This abstract is a summary of the paper with the same title, Theoretical estimation of a strongly linked Dirac metal.

Power spectrum analysis via periodogram calculation is a widely used
method for detecting periodic signals in astronomical data, but its effectiveness
can be limited by a critical frequency leakage problem. Traditional methods
attempt to mitigate this issue by dividing the data into shorter segments and
averaging their results, although these approaches can still be flawed. They
usually rely on a fixed number of data samples proportional to the desired
period and fail to consider the specific characteristics of the signal. We present
a novel method that normalizes the data by a suitable interval containing
the desired period, allowing for maximum control over frequency and period
settings. This method demonstrates its superiority over standard techniques in
real-world applications. Furthermore, it facilitates a more intuitive
understanding of frequency spectra by normalizing the x-axis, and our method
can be used with both unimodal and bimodal frequency spectra. We provide our
method's code for public use. 

In order to evaluate our method's performance, we utilized two established
signals with known characteristics, along with two artificial bimodal signals
and one real-life bimodal phenomenon. Our method outperformed traditional
techniques in all cases.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework, named Self-Aligned Dual Face Prediction Network (SADRNet), which produces two face predictions: one based on the visible facial region and the other based on inferred hidden facial structures. These predictions are then combined to achieve a comprehensive 3D face reconstruction. Exhaustive testing of our method has shown that it excels in both dense alignment and reconstruction tasks, achieving exceptional results on the FRFB5000 dataset and outperforming a top conference-based method by a margin of 8.16% (25.29-17.13) in terms of reconstruction metric NMDS. The method's source code has been made freely available online for reference purposes. Adjustments to the original protocol, which involved increasing the size of the training dataset to 8,000 samples, were found to further improve SADRNet's performance, resulting in a further reduction of 2.16% (25.29-23.13) when compared to the primary state-of-the-art approach. The method's exceptional performance is significant, given the significant challenges associated with real-world 3D face reconstruction applications such as video surveillance. Spontaneous symmetry breaking of the translation group occurs when uniform potentials are used in the $\phi^4$ model at its critical point. This phenomenon gives rise to equilibrium fluctuations in one and higher spatial dimensions that maintain uniformity. We investigate the consequences of explicitly violating the underlying symmetry by introducing uniform, static fields. This disruption results in divergent energy costs associated with certain fluctuations, known as fractons, whose properties we comprehensively examine across all dimensions. Furthermore, we explore the impact of these defects on decay rates and correlation lengths in the presence of both stable and unstable translations. The models we study exhibit similarities to those of discrete, one-dimensional systems with commensurate phases, but with key distinctions, particularly regarding the dimensions of fracton operators and the associated dimensionality of potential terms. The interplay between these dimensions, coupled with the underlying symmetry's spontaneous breaking, gives rise to the coexistence of power-like and exponential decay behaviors in one dimension. In higher dimensions, decay rates are determined by the dimensionality of charge propagation alone. The models we examine also highlight the distinct, anisotropic nature of charge propagation in one dimension, with distinct decay rates being influenced by both spatial and temporal dimensions. The anisotropy results in distinct, cross-compatible dimensions of various physical properties, with some being the same in one dimension as in higher dimensional, isotropic systems. The models we study can be applied to systems with near-neighbor interactions in one dimension, where the disruption of translation invariance can be seen as shifting the model's equilibrium, uniform potential. The consequences of this shift are shown to result in the systems' dual, double-wound, multi-component representations, with both stable and unstable translations being similarly affected. The models we study can also be examined in the presence of an external, time-varying electric field, with the disruption of translation invariance being achieved through the introduction of temporal, static fields. This leads to the introduction of multi-component, double-wound representations in both spatial and temporal dimensions, with the resulting, efficient field theories exhibiting both charged and charge-neutral components that maintain uniformity. The resulting, double-wound representations give rise to the coexistence of power-like and exponential decay behaviors in one dimension, with decay rates in higher dimensions being determined by the dimensionality of charge propagation alone. The models we study result in the, previously unreported phenomenon of 'hidden fractons', with systems at their critical points and under the influence of a external, time-varying electric field exhibiting power-like decay behavior.

The rapid dissemination of music videos on TikTok and the prominence of "audiotrains" in modern societies pose significant challenges. Current misinformation research is hampered by a lack of empirical data from these environments. This study investigated the spread of harmful audio on TikTok and the effects it has on young people. A popular music track with a embedded deadly virus warning audio was analyzed alongside a visually appealing video featuring a popular dance. The video was shared on TikTok among 1500 participants, aged 16-25, and viewed up to 10 times by each user. The results showed that both enjoyable content and social connections motivated users to view the video, with 72% of them sharing it with others. This research provides valuable insights into the spread of harmful audio on TikTok and highlights the need for more effective warning messages that can reach a wider audience. Due to the significant implications of these findings, the study recommends developing and executing pruning-based warning strategies on TikTok and similar platforms. The rise of continuously expanding image databases like ImageNet has created a need for a more effective approach to learning from data. Traditionally, the distributional assumptions present in fixed datasets pose a problem due to their limitations, but this obstacle disappears with an endlessly growing dataset that reflects real-world visual data. This theoretical advancement can further enhance the practical benefits of incremental learning, eliminating the need to choose specific training data and allowing for unlimited growth without the memory constraints of previous datasets. This paper introduces a Dynamic Learning method that addresses fundamental challenges in deep learning, including optimization, overfitting, and the representation of visual data, and provides unprecedented achievements on benchmark datasets like CIFAR-10, MNIST, and ImageNet, reducing the number of shots required by orders of magnitude compared to existing techniques. Notably, it achieves a top-1 accuracy of 73.0% on the full ImageNet dataset with just 125,000 samples, surpassing the performance of a model trained on the entire dataset with 1.4 billion samples. This method has numerous applications, including the training of models for real-time deployment, the creation of more challenging benchmark datasets, and the development of a unified framework for both static and dynamic learning techniques. This approach has important implications for the field of machine learning, particularly in natural language processing, where similar large-scale datasets are sure to follow in the future. Despite being influenced by both magnetic field and current, the zero-current Hall resistance of superconductors exhibits a striking symmetry. We have investigated the impact of vacancies on the Hall anomaly in BSCCO using a fixed lattice of vortices and examined the irregularity of the Hall effect through a quantitative measure. The findings show that a linear relationship exists between the Hall anomaly and the vacancy gradient, and that the irregularity is directly proportional to the vacancy gradient and inverse to the square root of applied magnetic field. This leads to an increase in irregularity with increasing current above a certain threshold, which we attribute to the non-uniform distribution of supercurrent. This understanding may be useful for optimizing the Hall effect in superconducting materials. We observe two different values of proportionality constants, likely resulting from differences in pinning mechanisms, and note that the smaller constant appears more relevant in practical applications. Furthermore, our study reveals that the Hall anomaly is more pronounced in the center of the thin film, and the use of a linear regression analysis to validate our theoretical model for the Hall anomaly. This model demonstrates that the Hall anomaly is a universal function of the applied magnetic field and the vacancy gradient, and we propose future experiments to investigate the effects of lattice distortions and normal-superconducting interfaces on the Hall anomaly. A commuting square of von Neumann algebras, characterized by a specific set of finite-dimensional matrices, is used to derive a subfactor with a known depth. The structure of the square, represented by the matrix $\Gamma$, plays a significant role in determining the index and depth of the resulting subfactor. A method to identify squares with optimal depth was established through advances in bivariational theory. Our research introduces an alternative approach to describing such squares with optimal depth, focusing on the properties of the associated $\Gamma$ matrix. A more intuitive understanding of these squares is derived from a different perspective, utilizing the concept of integer partitions. This perspective enables the derivation of squares with optimal depth in various index levels. A specific notation system is introduced to represent the structure of these squares, characterized by the configuration of integer partitions. This notation facilitates a more explicit description of the basis vectors and the composition of the square. The action of the square's operators can be more clearly defined using this notation, deriving new insights into its underlying morphology. A specific square with an index of three is presented as an illustrative example, featuring a Morita equivalent that includes a tower of squares with optimal depth. This tower, resulting from a series of unitary evaluations, demonstrates its connection to the Haagerup approximation, a fundamental process. Our research also explores the application of unitary evaluations to a specific square with an index of four, derived from the analysis of a tower of squares with optimal depth. This unitary-derived square exhibits an increased depth of six, offering a more complex structure than its predecessors. A distinct feature of our introduced squares with optimal depth is the presence of a finite-dimensional commuting square that generates the subfactor, derived from a unitary evaluation of the hyperfinite type II_1 factor, denoted as $N \subset B(H)$. To encourage listening, music bloggers write engaging summaries of playlists.
These summaries not only motivate listeners to explore the playlist but also aid in discovering new music.

This paper focuses on enhancing the quality of summaries produced by neural network models for this task.

It demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to a diverse music dataset consisting of over 140,000 tracks and featuring over 16,000 tracks in over 8,000 playlists, with human evaluators confirming that the presented models outperformed the original transformer encoder in terms of summary quality. Current methods often rely on frame-wise prediction, extending into supplementary context frames beyond actual action duration. We introduce a new approach, we call Dual Context Action Network (DCAN), which enhances temporal action recognition by limiting model predictions to specific action duration frames. We preclude the necessity of predicting additional context frames, reducing necessary action context by half. To achieve this, two context integrations are incorporated into DCAN: 1) internal context integration, combining core action frames with surrounding context frames encoded by the spatial attention module, and 2) external context integration, integrating distant context frames encoded by the spatial attention module with core action frames. We subject our method to extensive evaluation, obtaining superior or competitive results on five benchmark datasets. We also include detailed studies on crucial parameters and methods. Specifically, we utilize Control Barrier Functions with input restrictions to safely steer the system towards a secure target state. To achieve this, we first reformulate the safe reachability issue as a problem of satisfying the control barrier condition across subsequent time steps. Then, we extract the essential ingredients for our approach, including the identification of control barrier states and formation of feasible control inputs to navigate the system through time-stamped secure areas. For both cases, we outline the procedures for calculating control barrier states and constructing input policies to ensure safe reachability. Our results are validated through numerical experiments using the underactuated pendulum and the Inertial Measurement Unit systems, and our approach is found to effectively manage systems with noisy deterministic and stochastic dynamics, respectively. This study evaluates the effectiveness of next-generation electron-positron colliders at identifying the Higgs boson in its native environment. Considering that new physics beyond the Standard Model might manifest through the Effective Field Theories at energy scales well above the Standard Model's sensitivity threshold, we focus on the EFT description of the Higgs sector. Specifically, we analyzed the relevance of higher-dimensional operators influencing the Higgs coupling, the self-interaction, and the relationship between the Higgs and a vector boson within a context where the operator's impact is minimal (the "weak effective field theory" applicable in the TeV range). Our primary concern is the double Higgs production process in these colliders and how it relates to the sensitivity of these instruments to new physics. We investigated this process in several scenarios, both with and without new physics contributions at an energy scale of up to 10 TeV, and compared them to a 100 TeV hadron collider for reference. Our analysis reveals that a 250-TeV, 0.5-TeV collider can replicate a significant portion of a 100-TeV hadron collider's capability and that the most sensitive areas for this process are in the forward regions of the detector. Furthermore, we established that a 250-TeV, 0.5-TeV collider can yield results for certain operator coefficients with a margin of error as small as 0.013, and that it can detect a 20% deviation in the trilinear Higgs interaction at a 3-sigma confidence level with a 10-TeV energy reach. This study also examines the potential for these colliders to distinguish between different new physics scenarios that could result in similar patterns of Higgs production and that it lays the groundwork for a more comprehensive analysis of the interplay between Higgs pair production and single Higgs production in these colliders. The underlying mechanics of granular drag anisotropy remain only partially understood, largely because measuring this phenomenon is very challenging. To tackle this issue, a robust apparatus was designed that allows cylindrical objects to move freely within a plane of friction, thereby enabling the measurement of drag anisotropy in various directions. Utilizing this apparatus, the effects of water on drag anisotropy were investigated by comparing the results for dry sand and sand saturated with water. The data show that the anisotropic component of drag forces is significant, accounting for as much as 75% of the total drag force. The direction of maximum drag resistance is found to be precisely 60 degrees away from the direction of motion, a finding consistent with previous research conducted on slender objects moving through a fluid. However, the most noteworthy discovery is that the anisotropic component of drag forces is largely unaffected by the presence of water, a finding with implications for the design of cylindrical vehicles that operate in both dry and wet conditions. The data also highlight the importance of considering the speed at which drag forces are measured, as slower speeds result in more erratic readings. To facilitate the reproduction of these results, the code used for data analysis and simulations is made openly available. Additionally, the code can be modified to model the motion of objects moving in a plane of friction, as well as in other complex environments. Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a starburst galaxy Abell 1604, focusing on its central 4-kiloparsec area. Our data show an extremely large molecular gas outflow in Abell 1604, extending beyond 3.5 kiloparsecs from the center, which is unusual for an outflow. We discovered that this outflow's extreme size may be linked to star formation suppression at the same spatial range. Our analysis indicates that the outflow could be related to the central supermassive black hole, and we found a massive rotating accretion disk, but no sign of an active galactic nucleus. Based on our findings, we suggest that there's a hidden population of buried active galactic nuclei or a highly irregular, "hybrid" structure in this system. We also present radio continuum evidence of a potentially interacting galaxy pair, suggesting that Abell 1604 might be in its final stages of major galaxy merger. Our observations with KCWI show an irregularly shaped, bursty star formation pattern in the central area of Abell 1604, and we detected several giant H II regions and a massive young stellar bulge. Our results support the idea that massive, rotating gas disks, which allow for both inflow and outflow, can lead to enhanced star formation rates and account for the star formation variability observed in some galaxy populations. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the physics and chemistry in a highly variable, starburst galaxy and offers a new perspective on the "diet" of such galaxies, suggesting that outflows play a key role in controlling the development of their accretion disks and star formation. A demonstration of KCWI's capabilities, our observations highlight the instrument's ability to capture high-resolution, high-sensitivity observations of a galaxy's central area. A demonstration of NOEMA's capabilities, our observations showcase the instrument's ability to obtain high-sensitivity, resolved observations of a galaxy's molecular gas. Our observations with these instruments not only provide a new perspective on the physics and chemistry in a highly variable, starburst galaxy but also highlight the exceptional performance of KCWI and NOEMA. Our observations with these instruments also demonstrate their capability to capture a combination of optical and submillimeter data on a galaxy, paving the way for further studies in astronomy. Our study of Abell 1604, a highly variable, starburst galaxy, may serve as a model for conducting further research on other galaxy populations and as a new standard for the comprehensive study of a galaxy

Our research examined the occurrence of triangular flow in A+A collisions using the multiphase transport model, and found that it originates from interactions between participants and the anisotropic mean-field scalar field. We investigated how this anisotropic effect varies with different colliding systems and energy levels. Specifically, we analyzed the scalar flow's anisotropy in the transverse plane for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Our results showed that the scalar flow's anisotropy in the midrapidity region is higher in Cu+Cu collisions than in Au+Au collisions, due to the larger mean-field anisotropy in smaller systems. However, when normalized by the number of participants, the anisotropy in midrapidity is similar for Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions, indicating that the mean-field anisotropy's influence on triangular flow depends on the interaction between participants. We also found the scalar flow to be negative in central collisions, and its magnitude increases with the number of participants in noncentral collisions. Furthermore, we examined the scalar flow's component parallel to the line of collision, and discovered that it contributes to triangular flow only in noncentral collisions. We additionally studied the scalar flow's angular distribution and identified two components: one related to the line of collision and the other to the orthogonal direction. When integrating over the entire transverse plane, the orthogonal component dominates the scalar flow's anisotropy. We found the orthogonal component's anisotropy to be similar for Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions when normalized by the number of participants. We investigated the scalar flow's connection to triangular flow and found their coefficients to be proportional to one another. We explored possible experimental signatures of the scalar flow with forward neutral pion multiplicity and fourth-order anisotropy coefficients. When working with random processes monitored at finite intervals, as is common in scientific studies, determining parameter values can be complicated due to the discrete nature of the data. This difficulty is exacerbated by the limited amount of data typically collected, which further hinders the usual precision of estimates. In such cases, conventional methods like the maximum likelihood estimator fail both theoretically, due to a high dependence on sampling frequency, and practically, because they involve computationally intensive calculations for a single parameter model. This paper explores a novel, feasible method for calculating maximum likelihood estimates in models that involve hidden variables, offering a practical solution for a range of statistical models commonly applied to discrete data sets. The proposed approach yields effective and efficient results, as demonstrated by data analysis and computational experiments conducted across multiple fields. It significantly reduces the computational time, achieving a factor of $10^4$ to $10^5$ times improvement over standard methods. The new approach exhibits a precision of at least $50\%$ more than existing methods, under typical monitoring conditions. Furthermore, it facilitates calculation of the standard error, although with less accuracy than continuous methods. The proposed method shows particular usefulness in estimating models that describe observed means and autocorrelation coefficients. It can be applied to models with a wide range of parameter values, as well as to data sets with both stationary and non-stationary characteristics. The algorithm is highly versatile, as demonstrated by its ability to handle multiple starting points, resulting in at least $50\%$ more accurate estimates than Bayesian methods. This paper offers a computational framework for a wide range of maximum likelihood estimation problems, as well as a publicly accessible implementation of the proposed algorithm. The development of highly advanced autonomous vehicles depends heavily on the creation of realistic traffic simulation tools. Current methods for generating realistic traffic scenes rely on extensionally defined rules which can be limited in capacity and tend to produce scenes lacking in variety. To address these issues, we propose SceneGen, a novel traffic scene generator that utilizes both graph-based techniques and text-based rich templates. By utilizing a combination of template-based constraints and semi-supervised learning, SceneGen is able to produce highly realistic and diverse traffic scenes that are both visually and metrically accurate. When evaluated against real-world scenes, SceneGen demonstrates SceneGen's ability to create authentic and diverse traffic scenes. The model's code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/daoyu-cpu/Scenegen. Modern cloud computing employs microservices architecture with multiple containerized services. 

Despite the benefits, unsecured microservices pose a significant threat if compromised by malware, as a system call backward hook can allow attackers to bypass container security and cause severe damage.

Existing solutions for securing containers against malware rely on heavy-weight virtualization, static analysis, or trusted hardware, which are either inefficient or impractical for large-scale deployment.

This research introduces a novel approach, called Timeloops, a lightweight learning-based method for predicting malicious system calls in future time loops. 

It combines a new call-pattern extraction algorithm with a novel future-time-loop prediction model, using a combination of static and dynamic data, and is designed for efficient execution even in small containers.

Evaluations using real-world malware and services demonstrate Timeloops' high accuracy, low performance overhead, and ability to detect over 85% of malicious system calls in future time loops with just 0.25 seconds of training. 

The project is also open-sourced, allowing for exploration and integration into popular container runtimes and security frameworks. 
It is also shown that Timeloops can significantly outperform state-of-the-art security solutions for container security. 
The research is further extended to detect RCE vulnerabilities in code with little overhead, and this is demonstrated with evaluations using real-world malware and services. 
The approach is generalizable, transparent, and integrates seamlessly with existing container runtimes, making it an ideal low-overhead learning-based security framework for modern cloud computing.

Historical sundials served as primary timekeepers before the invention of mechanical clocks, with many countries utilizing them for over a thousand years. To better comprehend the cultural development and technological advancements of ancient societies, researchers developed the Suryakala-Nusantara application, which enables users to record sundial data including shadow lengths, allows for the calculation of local standard time, and incorporates an interactive calendar feature.  By collecting sundial observations, users can contribute to a comprehensive database of sunrise, noon, and sunset times while gaining insights into their local environment.  The application also provides statistical analysis of collected data, identifying trends and anomalies, and incorporating graphical representations for easier interpretation.  With a focus on Indonesia, the application includes detailed information about Indonesian sundials, along with an engaging educational component and a social platform for users to connect and share their experiences. By allowing the attention module to select specific feature locations for input to the classifier, AttDLNet significantly enhances performance and efficiency compared to existing methods. Experimental results show that our model achieves exceptional accuracy at low latency, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches like PointRCNN and LagNet at a fraction of the computational cost. Furthermore, we find that LiDARS with more points result in improved performance but also increase processing time, necessitating a balance between data density and processing requirements. The code for AttDLNet has been made publicly available on GitHub. Moreover, we introduce a novel evaluation metric called the location recognition density (LRD), measuring a method's efficacy in accurately identifying locations across different LiDAR densities, and demonstrate the superiority of AttDLNet under this benchmark. The proposed model's efficiency, combined with its exceptional performance and ability to effectively process a range of LiDAR densities, makes it an ideal candidate for real-world applications. Furthermore, we discover that AttDLNet's focus-based attention mechanism provides unique insights into selecting relevant feature locations for classification, a previously unexplored aspect of point cloud data. The Aberdeen Tunnel is located in Dumbarton, Scotland, within the Leven estuary. It spans 215 meters in length and maintains a consistent, flat cross-section. This section is separated from the main tank by a 100-meter-long pipe, known as the "proton beam line."

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy sensitivity are not yet fully understood, despite extensive research on this topic. Recent evidence suggests that animacy perception is highly interconnected with other visual perceptions, such as object recognition and action perception. However, the animacy perception mechanism in VTC remains distinct and independent. Our study employs linear decomposition of multi-variate data to demonstrate the uniqueness of the VTC animacy pathway. We found that the combination of features from object, action and other areas in inferior temporal (IT) and medial superior temporal (MST) cortices fails to capture the animacy signature in VTC. Conversely, a separate set of features in IT, MST and other areas is required to explain the data, suggesting that the animacy mechanism in VTC operates independently. This conclusion is further supported by the observation that the animacy sensitivity in VTC is highly selective to living agents with intentional action, consistent with a theory of intentional agent (IT-A) representation. We also showed that this intentional agent representation is present across different stimulus modalities, including vision, sound and haptic, and is fundamental to human animacy perception. Furthermore, our analysis identified key visual and non-visual features that characterize this IT-A representation, comprising spatial organization, face presence, body presence, motion, sound source localization and agency, among others. These features form an animacy structure that underpins human animacy perception, providing a framework for the comprehension of intentional behavior in various forms of life, including single agents, groups of agents, and animate environments. Moreover, our research demonstrates that this animacy structure is an emergent, high-level construct derived from the combination of lower-level feature representations of visual and non-visual agents, rather than a hardwired code. Finally, our study demonstrates that this intentional agent representation is uniquely human, as distinct from the animacy perception mechanisms observed in other primates. These findings offer a new theoretical framework for the complex mechanism of human animacy perception, one that can inform future neurobiological research and provide a foundation for addressing broader questions regarding the human brain's capacity for abstract conceptual thinking. Additionally, our study demonstrates that this intentional agent representation is an key component of human social intelligence, shaped by both genetic and environmental factors, with significant implications for our understanding of the human animacy system, social cognition, and the unique human experience. Furthermore, our research provides a foundation for exploring the neural basis of human morality, empathy, and a wide range of other human behaviors that are driven by human animacy

However, current artificial neural networks require extensive retraining when adapting to different problems, despite having an extensive amount of unsampled data available from across the internet. This project explores the idea of allowing neural networks to generalize across different tasks without being trained on the specific data, and the conditions necessary for this to be achievable, as evidenced by our successful application of this concept to the problem of image classification. A key insight of this project is that successful cross-task generalization relies on a combination of two factors: first, the ability of the network to extract fundamental features that are common to all tasks and remain stable even when the input data changes; second, the use of a memory system that allows the network to draw on its past experience when processing new input data. This memory system, specifically a retrieval module, allows the network to recover important details that were initially missed during its initial, unsupervised training, and allows it to switch to solving a different problem more easily. This is supported by a thorough analysis of different network architectures and the results of our experiments, which show that the best approaches to cross-task generalization involve a combination of a simple, unsophisticated network architecture that is easy to train and a sophisticated memory system. Our research found that the most influential users in promoting rumors had typically k-core values between 1 and 3, and often used direct messaging to encourage the spread of information. The analysis of themes in online rumors revealed a diverse range of topics, often unrelated to COVID-19, with many focusing on societal issues. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of online rumor propagation in China during the pandemic, with implications for the design of counter-measures to control the spread of unhealthy information. Furthermore, we highlight the value of our approach to studying online rumors in real-world settings, while also emulating the conditions experienced during the COVID-19 period. This distortion can affect the path of neutrinos emitted during the collapse, potentially interfering with neutrino detectors' ability to identify a neutrino burst originating from a collapsing black hole. Furthermore, the distorted neutrino emission spectrum may vary significantly depending on the star's initial composition and orientation, presenting an intriguing opportunity for neutrino astronomy to determine the collapsing star's properties and distinguish it from a merging neutron-star binary event. Additionally, the unique characteristics of collapse neutrino spectra may allow for differentiation from merger neutrino spectra, offering a hopeful basis for multi-messenger observations in the future. The modeling of collapse and merge events side by side may provide a better understanding of the underlying physics and improve detection signatures of both neutrino sources. The modeling of collapse events in our research focuses specifically on the production of neutrinos and electromagnetic radiation from the formation of a accretion disk around a rotating black hole, highlighting the significance of spin in the detection of these events. However, it also raises the question of what other general relativity effects are missed by considering a simplified, overlying framework. In rehabilitative games, models of a player's impaired control are used to adjust levels of difficulty, however these models often lack a clear theoretical foundation. By drawing from control systems and rehabilitation expertise, we make the case that a specific class of stochastic dynamic games offers valuable insights and framework for structuring rehabilitative content. We demonstrate how a particular solution to these games can produce challenging and engaging experiences, as well as provide restorative benefits, by leveraging impairments in a way that promotes exploration and learning. Through the development of a rehabilitative driving game for individuals with Parkinson's disease, we show that a carefully designed set of restorative parameters can boost cognitive benefits and that a similar approach could be applied to other types of impairment. We also introduce the concept of an "impairment envelope" that can be used to prioritize gaming restoration through the placement of obstacles that require restoration in order to be overcome. By incorporating this idea into the design of a rehabilitative space navigation game, we found that it led to more efficient restoration of challenging levels, as well as resulting in higher scores when regular games are played on the same platform. We believe that viewing player control through the lens of control theory has the potential to greatly enhance the development of rehabilitative games. We have made the code for these experiments available online. Furthermore, we have introduced the concept of "restoration vectors" that can be used to adjust the difficulty of rehabilitative games in a more precise and flexible manner, and have explored the potential for machine learning approaches to be used to create more accurate models of a player's control, as well as how they can be incorporated into the development of rehabilitative games. We have also begun to investigate the potential for cross-game transfer of benefits, and have made the code for these experiments available online. We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in third-generation gauge vector leptoquarks, specifically a charge of $U_3(2,1)$, within the context of QCD at next-to-leading order in the strong coupling plus the exact matrix element at leading order. This analysis is applicable to Drell-Yan production of same-flavour or opposite-flavour lepton pairs across a wide mass range, from domain-wall effects up to the mass threshold, and is executed with the help of Matchbox, a grid-based matching framework. Our study reveals that next-to-leading order corrections in QCD significantly enhance the precision of predictions, especially in heavy leptoquark mass scenarios, and that the choice of renormalisation and factorisation scales has a notable impact on the results, with an influence of several GeV in certain cases. Furthermore, we observe that the inclusion of two-loop colour dipole terms in the soft matrix element leads to a reduction in the residual scale uncertainty to below 5%, and that the predicted cross-section at this precision is consistent with the available literature in the high-mass limit. The development of vector leptoquark effective field theories within the context of QCD at next-to-leading order in the strong coupling plus the exact matrix element at leading order is also explored in this study. Research facilities like the Paul Scherrer Institute's (PSI) neutron spallation source require highly accurate measurements of neutron cross-sections to ensure effective operation. While existing detectors have limitations such as poor energy resolution and significant background interference, a novel 3D-projection scintillator detector was developed to overcome these challenges. By utilizing a thick scintillator instead of individual detectors for energy and tracking, this design offers enhanced energy resolution, improved angular resolution, and reduced background through the identification of stopping particles. For example, measuring the neutron cross-section on carbon at 672 MeV, a threshold previously inaccessible due to background issues, became feasible with this new detector design. With a energy resolution of 1.82 MeV and virtually no background above this limit, it was possible to obtain reliable results. The developed detector was used to determine the cross-section on carbon at this energy and several others above the threshold, namely at 672, 693, 703, 705, 706, 707, 708, and 709 MeV. The results show a strong correlation with world references for energies where existing detectors had already obtained reliable data, and the novel detector also demonstrated its capability to detect exclusive and semi-exclusive reactions. Furthermore, the unique characteristics of the 3D-projection scintillator detector make it an ideal choice for detecting exclusive and semi-exclusive reactions across a wide range of energies. As in the previous study, we found that at higher temperatures, the presence of a water-rich environment leads to increased sticking forces, although this increase is less pronounced than at lower temperatures. However, we also discovered that in a water-rich environment, sticking forces actually decrease as temperature rises, which could be a result of the evaporation of water at high temperatures or the loss of a water-rich coating as particles collide. This effect might allow particles to collide multiple times and stick together more than once. Additionally, we observed that in a water-rich environment, sticking forces are similar when temperature is high but the water is frozen versus when temperature is low but the water is melted, which has implications for the growth of particles in a protoplanetary disc, particularly in regions where temperatures rise after dust grains move closer to the sun. This, in turn, suggests that particles can still stick together and grow as they move inward, a process that could lead to the formation of large particles and even planetesimals through streaming instability. This research was done in collaboration with the University of Oxford, the University of Manchester, and the University of Edinburgh. This work is relevant to the ongoing JPCOR project and will be discussed further in the paper. It is also being presented as a oral presentation at the 68th Meeting of the Astronomical Society of Japan in October 2022 and will be published in the Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan in October 2023. Researchers explored the usage of machine learning through a simple neural network called a Single-Pixel Convolutional Neural Network, integrating it with the Fermi All-sky Survey. This survey includes extensive data on gamma rays from the sky, monitored over 10 years, allowing for a massive 8,000-fold reduction in data from 3,000 images. This achievement facilitates the identification of rare sources within the data without relying on pre-selected target areas. To further streamline the process, a basic image enhancement technique known as contrast stretching was applied to the reduced data, yielding promising results for the automatic detection of sources like active galactic nuclei from black holes. 

The implementation of this method on the reduced data revealed 15 new source candidates with significantly increased contrast, including some that match known variable sources, such as X-ray binaries and pulsars. However, further verification is needed to confirm these findings through direct measurements from the Fermi-LAT. The method also discovered regions of the sky that exhibit significant variability compared to the overall survey, amounting to several thousand candidates. 

Despite advancements in sensor technology, the current Fermi-LAT camera retains high sensitivity to detecting gamma rays, as demonstrated by its ability to identify sources like X-ray binaries that emit relatively low energy levels, up to 100 GeV. However, the camera's limited field of view means that only a small percentage of its sensitivity is utilized for typical observations. 

The research team applied their machine learning model to a broader spectrum of gamma rays, considering not just point sources but also large-scale structures and phenomena from the cosmos. The resulting output showed enhanced contrast and revealed potential variable sources, highlighting the effectiveness of combining machine learning with extensive astronomical data sets. Further studies are needed to validate and refine their findings, with potential applications to other astronomical surveys and the optimization of telescope observations. Furthermore, this approach may facilitate the discovery of new variable sources and celestial structures within these data sets. 

The employed machine learning framework excels at processing complex, real-world images and can be adapted to other astronomical images, enabling the sharpness enhancement of such images and potential identification of sources and structures, as demonstrated on the Fermi All-sky Survey. This study paves the way for the exploration of other high-energy astronomical data sets using machine learning, such as those from X-ray and gamma-ray telescopes, and the incorporation of expert knowledge into the model to accurately model specific source types and celestial structures.

The majority of near-Earth asteroids are expected to consist of binary or fragmented objects.  To investigate this further, our study turns to Pan-STARRS1's extensive image database from the past decade, utilizing their unique PS1-$CAIPER$ detector with low optical cross-section of approximately 49 arcseconds squared. Our analysis involves examining 697 asteroid discoveries within 1 million kilometers of the Earth's orbit and analyzing potential second components of near-Earth asteroids.  For each detected asteroid, we conducted 13 deep reductions of images from the past decade, removing non-asteroid objects and eliminating false positives through high confidence samples from the Palomar-QCOL and Catalina surveys, ultimately estimating the detection probability of binary asteroids.  Based on our analysis of 89 main belt and 34 near-Earth asteroids and considering factors like orbital period, eccentricity and tidal constraints, our findings suggest that binary asteroids with wide orbital separations may have a detection rate more than twice as likely as their non-binary counterparts, offering a preliminary insight into the binary population of near-Earth and main belt asteroids.  The research presented here is a preliminary analysis of data, a more in-depth discussion of methods and a broader context of the results will be explored in a companion paper.  In the context of current research, our study provides evidence for binary asteroids within the near-Earth population and addresses limitations and potential improvements for future binary asteroid detections.  As such, our study can serve as a guiding example for researchers using similar approaches with future surveys and more extensive image databases from projects such as ATLAS, ZTF, and Gaia.  As a result, our study has implications for the broader field of asteroid research and will continue to contribute to a more in-depth understanding of the population of binary asteroids across the solar system.  Furthermore, our study has a practical application for researchers allocating time on telescopes such as ATLAS, ZTF, and Gaia, as a demonstration of the value of historical image analysis and potential discoveries that can be made with even a limited allocation of time on these surveys.  As such, our study will also serve as a reference point for a proposal to allocate time on the ATLAS telescope, specifically in analyzing the recently discovered asteroid (2021 DB, Mars grazer) and potential binary asteroids within the near-Earth population.  This will serve as a follow-up to the research presented here, as a demonstration of the detection rate of binary asteroids and the effectiveness of using historical image analysis with more extensive image databases

Researchers in astronomy typically rely on a variety of visualizations to effectively communicate complex data and research findings to both the scientific community and the general public. To facilitate rapid, high-quality visualizations, a suite of online tools has been adapted for astronomical applications and is now available for public use. These customized tools enable easy creation of images, spectra, light curves, and other graphical representations from various astronomical data formats, including VOTs, Tables, and Light Curves. To further enhance their functionality, a modified version of these tools has been updated and is now accessible through an easy-to-remember URL shortener. Additionally, the source code for these tools has been made openly available on GitHub, where it can be downloaded from the specified repository. To assist others in adopting these tools, a step-by-step guide on utilizing RCSEDv2 has also been created and is available on the AAS Code Gallery. RCSEDv2 is the result of a development project funded by the AAS, and it is available for use at http://rcsed.vosgi.fr. Leveraging RCSEDv2 is also possible by downloading the customized version available on GitHub. Furthermore, to facilitate seamless integration with presentation software, a set of pre-configured settings for the most popular options has been included with the package. RCSEDv2 is an open-source solution that allows users to create a wide range of visualizations, including images and spectra, light curves, and tables, utilizing various customization options and color schemes. With its user-friendly interface and extensive features, RCSEDv2 is an ideal tool for producing high-quality visualizations and animations, making it an invaluable resource for the scientific community. The Southern Atlantic ridge features a massive continental rift system that formed as a result of the separation of Africa and South America during plate divergence. This process began around 120 million years ago and has continued ever since, with distinct episodic patterns of extensional activity. Initially, the rifting phase was characterized by E-W directed extensional forces and corresponding fault patterns, however, approximately 85 million years ago, a significant shift occurred, where N-S directed extensional forces dominated, resulting in corresponding changes in fault orientation. Studies have attempted to analyze this phenomenon; some attributing it to changes in plate rotation direction, variations in thermal buoyancy, or forces generated by interaction with the African superplume. However, none of these theories have been extensively supported by data, and the Southern Atlantic remains a crucial region for better understanding continental rifting processes. This study reviews available geophysical and geological information to reconstruct the Southern Atlantic's history, identifying six distinct phases of tectonic activity, and proposes a hypothesis that explains the variation in episodic rifting patterns as result of different lunar tidal forces during various stages of the Earth's history. This hypothesis claims that changes in the Earth's elliptical orbit resulted in altered tidal forces, specifically those related to the 124.4-day lunar cycle, which in turn affected rifting rates by regulating magma supply. This hypothesis is supported by a strong correlation between the Earth's original eccentric orbit and the observed rifting patterns, and is a key factor that contributed to the final separation of the African and South American continents. This idea may also be applicable to other continental rifting systems, and the unique history of the Southern Atlantic makes it an ideal location for testing this hypothesis, which could provide a framework for a new lunar-tidal forced rifting model. A significant improvement in internal feature detection is demonstrated through experiments conducted on three diverse medical image datasets. Furthermore, the model's performance is comparable to leading boundary-focused and internal feature detection methods while requiring significantly less training data. Such a game would require both a deep understanding of characters' thoughts and intentions as well as their abilities and motivations. To explore this concept, we've developed a theoretical framework for a next-generation role-playing game based on the popular Dungeons and Dragons, incorporating elements of a game's narrative, social, and logical aspects. Our approach incorporates a set of desires, known as goals, which underlie all actions taken within the game, and we demonstrate how this framework enables more human-like interactions and a more engaging gaming experience. Additionally, we've designed multiple variants of this framework, each with varying levels of depth in both its intent and its understanding of other players' minds. We've tested these variants as part of a comprehensive evaluation of our AI Dungeon Master, focusing on its ability to successfully guide human players through challenging scenarios. Our results show that an almost perfect correlation exists between the depth of a player's understanding of the game's rules and their ability to complete difficult tasks, as well as a significant connection between the depth of a game's social complexity and the frequency of unsuccessful task attempts. Our analysis of the underlying forces driving these observations, along with our methodology and a more in-depth examination of the games involved in our experiments, are included within this handbook. We believe that exploring these findings will be valuable to both the broader gaming and the broader artificial intelligence communities. This determination enables us to derive an integral formula for the cross section in terms of the quasiparton distribution functions. A symplectic group making up the identity consists of those mapping that preserve $\omega$ and increase its scale to $r^2$. The composition of such mapping forms a Lie group denoted by $\mathrm{Symp}(\omega,r^2)$. A key aspect of this group is analyzed in this paper, specifically its local structure around the identity, as well as the geometric properties of its manifold. It's shown that if $r$ isn't equal to $1$, then this group has a unique local structure defined by two independent parameters near the identity, and that for $r=1$, it reduces to the identity component of the special linear group, $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$. Additionally, it's demonstrated that when $r\neq 1$, this group has a unique local structure defined by one parameter near the identity, and that it consists of the identity component of the group obtained by scaling the special linear group by a factor of $r^2$.
